# Exporting data {#sec-convert}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

library(rebook)
library(DT)
chapterPreamble(cache = FALSE)
```

There are two main ways to export data. The whole data container can be saved
to a file, which preserves all of its components and allows loading it back
later as the same object. Alternatively, the data can be exported as tables,
which can be opened with other tools, such as spreadsheet programs or other
programming languages, but which do not preserve the structure of the object.

## Save the data container {#sec-save-data-container}

### RDS files {#sec-rds}

The simplest way to save any R object, including `TreeSE` and
`MultiAssayExperiment`, is to write it to an RDS file with `saveRDS()`. The
file can be loaded back with `readRDS()`.

```{r}
#| label: save_rds
#| eval: false

data(GlobalPatterns, package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns

# Save TreeSE as an RDS file
saveRDS(tse, "path/to/tse.rds")

# Load the TreeSE back
tse <- readRDS("path/to/tse.rds")
```

RDS files are convenient for saving and reloading data in R, for example
between analysis sessions. However, they can only be read in R, and files
saved with old package versions are not always fully compatible with newer
versions. For long-term storage or for sharing data across tools, the
alabaster format described below is more robust.

### alabaster {#sec-alabaster}

The alabaster framework provides an alternative to RDS files. It saves the
data container as a directory of files in standard formats, which are not tied
to R. This makes the data easier to store long term and to share with other
programming languages. The `saveObject()` function writes the data to a
directory, and `readObject()` loads it back.

```{r}
#| label: alabaster
#| eval: false

# Requires the alabaster.treese package to be installed
library(alabaster)

# Save TreeSE into a directory
saveObject(tse, "path/to/tse")

# Load the TreeSE back
tse <- readObject("path/to/tse")
```

The same functions can be used to save and load `MultiAssayExperiment`
objects.

## Export as table {#sec-export-table}

### TreeSummarizedExperiment

Transforming a `TreeSE` object into a dataframe is straightforward with
the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` package. The `meltSE` function is
particularly handy for this purpose. It allows you to melt various parts
of a `TreeSE` object into a dataframe based on the parameters you specify.

Exporting a `TreeSE` data container can be done using the
`r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("feather")` package. The `TreeSE` object has to be
converted into a dataframe (`data.frame` and not `DataFrame`). The output
file is a .feather file, which can be imported in other languages such as
Julia or Python. For more information, have a look at the
[FeatherFile](https://juliapackages.com/p/featherfiles) Julia package and
[feather-format](https://pypi.org/project/feather-format/) Python
library.

```{r}
#| label: write_feather
#| eval: false

molten_tse <- meltSE(
    tse,
    add_row_data = TRUE,
    add_col_data = TRUE,
    assay.type = "counts"
)

# Export as a feather file
library(feather)
write_feather(molten_tse, "path/to/tse.feather")
```

Another way could be using a CSV file. This works the same as for a
feather file, make sure you have converted your `TreeSE` data container
as a dataframe. Note that you can decide whether you want to write
the row names or not.

```{r}
#| label: write_csv
#| eval: false

write.csv(molten_tse, "path/to/tse.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

To share the data with collaborators who work with spreadsheets, the
`se2xls()` function from the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SEtools")` package
writes a `TreeSE` to an Excel file without melting it first. The sample
data (`colData`), feature data (`rowData`) and each assay are saved on
separate sheets. Note that the phylogenetic tree is not included.

```{r}
#| label: write_xlsx
#| eval: false

library(SEtools)
se2xls(tse, filename = "path/to/tse.xlsx")
```

### MultiAssayExperiment

Exporting a `MultiAssayExperiment` data container can also be done using the
`r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("feather")` package.

```{r}
#| label: write_feather_mae
#| eval: false

# Convert into a data.frame
molten_mae <- longForm(mae)
molten_mae <- data.frame(molten_mae)
write_feather(molten_mae, "path/to/mae.feather")
```

And as a CSV file.

```{r}
#| label: write_csv_mae
#| eval: false

write.csv(molten_mae, "path/to/mae.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Export to standard data formats

Inspired by the
[rbiom vignettes](https://cmmr.github.io/rbiom/articles/convert.html),
`exportQIIME2()` and `exportMothur()` allow to save the data in a near-ready
format for analysis with QIIME2 and mothur, respectively. The output will need
additional processing in the target framework.

```{r}
#| label: write_qiime
#| eval: false

exportQIIME2(tse, "qiime2_folder")
```

Conversion is completed in the terminal using QIIME2. The output files can be converted to the standard QZA format as follows:

```bash
# Navigate to output folder
cd qiime2_folder

# Convert classic BIOM table to HDF5
biom convert -i counts.tsv -o counts.hdf5 --to-hdf5

# Convert counts to QZA
qiime tools import \
  --input-path counts.hdf5 \
  --type 'FeatureTable[Frequency]' \
  --input-format BIOMV210Format \
  --output-path counts.qza

# Convert taxonomy to QZA
qiime tools import \
 --input-path taxonomy.tsv \
 --type FeatureData[Taxonomy] \
 --output-path taxonomy.qza

# Convert tree to QZA
qiime tools import \
  --input-path tree.nwk \
  --type 'Phylogeny[Rooted]' \
  --output-path tree.qza
```

Alternatively, data can be exported to be used with mothur:

```{r}
#| label: write_mothur
#| eval: false

exportMothur(tse, "path/to/mothur_folder")
```

Again, conversion can be completed in the terminal using mothur:

```bash
# Navigate to output folder
cd mothur_folder

# Create shared file from counts table
mothur "#make.shared(count=counts.tsv, label=asv);"
```

In addition, the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("rbiom")` package can be used to export
the data in the BIOM format.

```{r}
#| label: write_biom
#| eval: false

# Convert TreeSE to BIOM
biom <- convertToBIOM(tse)

library(rbiom)
write_biom(biom, "path/to/tse.biom", format = "hdf5")
```

## Exercises

**Goal:** The goal is to learn how to convert the data format and how to
save the data.

**Exercise 1: Convert and save**

1. Load any of the example data sets described in [@sec-data-sets].

2. Convert data to a `phyloseq` object.

3. Convert the `phyloseq` data back to `TreeSE`.

4. Save a `TreeSE` object as a RDS file.

5. Read the RDS file into a `TreeSE` object.

6. Convert the data to long format and save it as a CSV file.

7. Export the data in a near-ready QIIME2 format

Useful functions:

`utils::data()`, `mia::convertToPhyloseq()`, `mia::convertFromPhyloseq()`,
`BiocGenerics::saveRDS()`, `base::readRDS()`, `mia::meltSE()`,
`utils::write.csv()`, `mia::exportQIIME2()`

:::
